content: 1. Upon admission, steps 1 through 4 should be completed on the same day as the patient’s presentation to ensure timely intervention. 2. Based on clinical assessment, initiate tuberculosis (TB) and opportunistic infection therapies immediately for patients who are critically ill. 3. The availability of point-of-care diagnostic tools, such as CD4 count, cryptococcal antigen (CrAg), lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay (LF-LAM), and viral load testing, facilitates rapid diagnosis, even in decentralized healthcare settings. 4. All patients presenting with headache or confusion and testing positive for CrAg should undergo a lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) for cryptococcal infection. 5. In settings where diagnostic results are quickly available, it is more cost-effective to test for cryptococcal infection before initiating TB treatment. 6. The algorithm for managing advanced HIV disease includes a comprehensive package of care, starting with history-taking and physical examination (Step 1). 7. Step 2 involves screening for symptoms of TB and meningitis. If meningitis symptoms are absent and the patient is not on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³, a blood CrAg test should be performed. 8. If the blood CrAg test is positive, and there are no contraindications, a lumbar puncture and CSF CrAg test should be conducted. Treatment should be guided by the results. 9. If diagnostic tests are unavailable and the patient is critically unwell, presumptive treatment for TB, cryptococcal meningitis, and bacterial meningitis should be considered. 10. If meningitis symptoms are present, perform blood CrAg testing, lumbar puncture, CSF CrAg testing, Xpert MTB/RIF assay, and microscopy. 11. If the CSF CrAg test is negative or a lumbar puncture is not feasible, initiate pre-emptive treatment for cryptococcosis. 12. If the CSF CrAg test is positive, begin treatment for cryptococcal meningitis. 13. Step 3 involves assessing for symptoms of meningitis, such as headache and confusion. 14. Step 4 focuses on treating other opportunistic infections and potential bacterial infections. Empiric treatment for pneumocystis pneumonia or bacterial pneumonia should be considered in patients with severe respiratory distress. 15. Step 5 recommends starting co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in accordance with WHO guidelines. 16. Step 6 evaluates whether the patient is already on ART. 17. Step 7 emphasizes providing intensified adherence support for opportunistic infection medications, ART, and monitoring the patient’s condition. Home visits and rapid tracing of patients who miss appointments should be considered. 18. Step 8 ensures effective communication for referral back to lower-level facilities after discharge to continue opportunistic infection and/or ART medications, initiate ART, or switch regimens as needed. 19. Task-sharing strategies may involve training non-laboratory staff, including lay health workers, to perform point-of-care diagnostics such as CD4 cell counts, CrAg testing, and urine LF-LAM testing at peripheral sites. 20. Nurse-led programs, supported by training and mentorship, can provide initial screening, TB treatment, opportunistic infection management, and prophylaxis. Clear referral criteria and care pathways must be established for higher-level clinical management when necessary. 21. For patients with advanced HIV disease, close follow-up during the initial period of ART is critical to monitor response and identify signs of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). 22. Weekly home visits during the first month of ART, as demonstrated in the REMSTART study, can improve outcomes. However, even with close follow-up, many patients die at home shortly after ART initiation, as observed in the REALITY trial. 23. Discharged patients with advanced HIV disease may require more intensive follow-up, with the frequency of visits tailored to the patient’s ability to travel to clinical sites. 24. Rapid tracing of patients who miss appointments should be conducted via phone or home visits. Where face-to-face contact is not feasible, alternative methods such as telephone consultations, mHealth interventions, or community health worker visits should be considered with the patient’s consent. 25. Programs should implement measures to improve linkage and follow-up after hospital discharge, such as outpatient primary care clinic visits and home visits by community health workers, to reduce the risk of loss to follow-up and mortality. 26. The package of care for advanced HIV disease should be provided to all eligible patients unless contraindicated. 27. Children older than five years with advanced HIV disease should receive the same package of care as adults. Children younger than five years are also eligible due to their high rates of severe immunosuppression and advanced clinical staging. 28. Major causes of mortality and morbidity in children with advanced HIV disease include TB, severe bacterial infections, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, while cryptococcal disease is rare. 29. Fixed-dose combinations of medications should be used for children to reduce pill or syrup burden, including co-trimoxazole, isoniazid, and pyridoxine. 30. Further research is needed to optimize the package of care for young children, particularly to address high rates of bacteraemia in infants under three months. 31. Adolescents with advanced HIV disease often face challenges with medication adherence, and enhanced adherence counseling is particularly valuable for this group. 32. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should receive nutritional support, disease prevention, and management of common physiological symptoms, as well as infant feeding support if breastfeeding is not possible. 33. People re-engaging with care after treatment interruption or failure should undergo a comprehensive clinical assessment and receive the advanced HIV disease package of care. 34. Patients on non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens who interrupt treatment are at risk of drug resistance and may require intensive virological monitoring. Switching to a non-NNRTI regimen should be considered to re-establish viral suppression. 35. Rapid viral load testing is recommended for patients with advanced HIV disease due to treatment failure. Where unavailable, clinical presentation should guide decisions on switching regimens. 36. Vaccination is an essential component of HIV care. However, severely immunosuppressed individuals may have reduced vaccine efficacy or higher risks with live attenuated vaccines. Additional doses or revaccination after immune reconstitution on ART may be necessary. 37. HIV-exposed infants, children, and adolescents should follow routine vaccination schedules with specific modifications. 38. The Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine should not be given to children with symptomatic HIV or unknown HIV status. 39. Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination should follow a three-dose schedule for immunocompromised individuals, regardless of ART status. 40. Measles vaccination should be administered to asymptomatic individuals and considered for symptomatic patients who are not severely immunosuppressed. Additional doses may be required after immune reconstitution. 41. Meningococcal vaccination is recommended for all individuals with immunodeficiency, including advanced HIV infection. 42. Pneumococcal vaccination may benefit infants and preterm neonates living with HIV, with booster doses in the second year of life. Routine adult vaccination with the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine is not recommended in resource-limited settings. 43. Inactivated polio vaccine or bivalent oral polio vaccine can be safely administered to asymptomatic infants with HIV. However, bivalent oral polio vaccine is contraindicated in severely immunocompromised individuals.
